maps.title: CA34S3 · 1. Performance management and the balanced scorecard

nodeData.topic: Performance management and the balanced scorecard
nodeData.note: How a business checks if it is doing well, and how it judges its managers fairly. You learn money measures (ROI, residual income, EVA), non-money measures, the balanced scorecard, and how targets change behaviour, including in hospitals, counties and other public bodies.

children.note: Start here: what performance management is and why owners and managers need it.
Performance management is setting goals, measuring results against them, and acting on the gaps. It links the plan (strategy) to what people do every day.

manas.q: What is performance management?

children.note: People work hard on whatever they are measured and paid on. So choosing the right measures is half the job.
A number that shows progress on something that really matters, for example bed occupancy in a hospital or sales per square metre in a supermarket.

manas.q: What is a key performance indicator (KPI)?

children.note: The few things a business must get right to win, such as fast service for a matatu SACCO. KPIs are then chosen to measure each CSF.

manas.q: What is a critical success factor (CSF)?

children.note: You already know budgets, standard costs and variances from CA25. Here we move up a level: judging whole divisions, managers and strategy, not single cost lines.
Big businesses split into parts. Each manager is judged only on what they control.
Giving each manager a part of the business and reporting results for that part. A manager is held to account only for what they can control.

manas.q: What is responsibility accounting?

children.note: The manager controls costs only, like a hospital laundry. Judge with budgets and cost variances.

manas.q: What is a cost centre?

children.note: The manager controls sales only, like a sales team. Judge on sales against target.
The manager controls both sales and costs, like one supermarket branch. Judge on profit.

manas.q: What is a profit centre?

children.note: The manager controls sales, costs AND decides on buying assets, like a whole regional division. Judge on ROI, residual income or EVA.

manas.q: What is an investment centre?

children.note: Controllable profit counts only costs the manager controls: use it to judge the manager. Traceable profit adds costs linked to the division but set by head office: use it to judge the division itself.

manas.q: Controllable profit or traceable profit: which judges the manager?

children.note: Local managers decide faster and know their market. The risk is that they chase their own division's results and hurt the group as a whole.

children.topic: Money measures: ROI, RI and EVA
children.note: The three main financial ways to judge an investment centre.
ROI = divisional profit ÷ capital employed in the division × 100%. It shows the profit earned on each shilling tied up in the division.

manas.q: What is the formula for ROI (divisional)?

children.note: Easy to understand and a percentage, so you can compare divisions of different sizes and compare with the cost of capital.
RI = divisional profit − (capital employed × cost of capital). It is the profit left after charging the division for the money it uses, in KES.

manas.q: What is the formula for residual income (RI)?

children.note: Any project earning more than the cost of capital raises RI, so managers take the right projects. You can also use a higher rate for riskier divisions.
A refined RI: net operating profit after tax (NOPAT) − (economic capital × WACC). Accounting figures are adjusted first, for example treating marketing and R&D as investment.

manas.q: What is economic value added (EVA)?

children.note: They use past accounting profit, can be boosted by cutting long-term spending, and say nothing about customers, quality or staff.
Why money measures alone can push managers the wrong way.
A division earning 15% may refuse a project earning 14%, even if the group's cost of capital is 12%. The group loses value. This is a lack of goal congruence.

manas.q: Why can ROI cause managers to reject good projects?

children.note: When what is good for the manager is also good for the whole company. Good measures create it; poor measures break it.

manas.q: What is goal congruence?

children.note: As assets are depreciated, net book value falls, so ROI rises with no real improvement. Managers may avoid replacing old equipment.
RI is a shilling figure, so a large division usually shows a bigger RI. You cannot compare divisions of different size fairly with RI alone.
All are one-year measures. A project with a loss in year 1 and big profits later looks bad now.
Measures that are not in shillings but often warn early of future profit or loss.
Measures of quality, time, customers, staff and innovation. Examples: waiting time, complaints, staff turnover, number of new products.

manas.q: What are non-financial performance indicators (NFPIs)?

children.note: They lead profit: unhappy patients today mean lost revenue next year. Front-line staff understand them and can act on them.
Patient waiting time in casualty, readmissions within 30 days, bed occupancy, patient satisfaction score, nurse turnover.
Trips per vehicle per day, on-time departures, accidents per 100,000 km, passenger complaints, M-Pesa share of fares.
Too many measures confuse people, some are hard to measure (like quality of care), and they can conflict with profit.
A tool that puts money and non-money measures on one page, linked to strategy.
Robert Kaplan and David Norton made it popular in the early 1990s, first in the Harvard Business Review. It is now used worldwide, in companies and in government.

manas.q: Who developed the balanced scorecard?

children.note: Judge the business from four angles, not money alone. Each angle has goals, measures, targets and actions, all linked to strategy.

manas.q: What is the balanced scorecard?

children.note: Kaplan and Norton ask four questions about the business.
How do we look to shareholders? Measures: ROI, RI, profit growth, cash flow, cost per patient.
How do customers see us? Measures: market share, satisfaction, repeat customers, complaints.
What must we be excellent at inside? Measures: speed, quality, error rates, waiting time, cost per process.
Can we keep improving and creating value? Measures: staff training hours, staff turnover, new services launched, IT systems.
Trained staff (learning) → faster, better processes (internal) → happier customers (customer) → more profit (financial). A strategy map draws this chain.
Balances short and long term, links daily work to strategy, and stops managers improving one area by damaging another.
Too many measures, hard to weigh one against another, costly to set up, and staff may resist being measured on new things.
Two more frameworks KASNEB may ask about briefly.
Fitzgerald and Moon, made for service businesses. Three blocks: dimensions (what to measure), standards (targets) and rewards.

manas.q: What are the three parts of the Fitzgerald and Moon building block model?

children.note: Results: financial performance and competitiveness. Determinants (causes of results): quality, flexibility, resource use and innovation.
Targets work best when staff feel ownership, find them achievable and see them as fair (equity) across managers.
Reward schemes should be clear, motivate people and be based only on things the manager controls.

Lynch and Cross link levels: corporate vision at the top, then market and financial goals, then customer satisfaction, flexibility and productivity, then quality, delivery, cycle time and waste at the base.

manas.q: What does the Lynch and Cross performance pyramid show?

children.note: Measures change how people act, not always for the better.
Actions that make a manager look good on the measure but harm the business, for example cutting maintenance to beat a cost target.

manas.q: What is dysfunctional behaviour in performance measurement?

children.note: Chasing this year's profit at the cost of the future: cutting training, R&D, marketing or repairs.

manas.q: What is short-termism?

children.note: Working only on what is measured. A hospital timed on casualty waiting may rush patients out too early.
Challenging but reachable, agreed with the manager, based on controllable items, and a mix of money and non-money.
Use several measures (balanced scorecard), judge over several years, reward with shares, and track long-term KPIs like staff skills.
Budget-constrained (strict focus on hitting budget), profit-conscious (focus on long-term results) and non-accounting (budget plays a small part).
Hospitals run by counties, NGOs and schools cannot be judged on profit alone.
Goals are many and sometimes vague (better health), there is no profit figure, and many stakeholders want different things.
Getting the most good from public money. It is judged with the 3Es: economy, efficiency, effectiveness.

manas.q: What is value for money (VFM)?

children.note: Buying inputs of the right quality at the lowest cost. Spending less on the same thing.

manas.q: What does economy mean in the 3Es?

children.note: Getting the most output from the inputs used: outputs ÷ inputs, like patients treated per nurse.

manas.q: What does efficiency mean in the 3Es?

children.note: How far the real goals are met: outcomes, not just outputs, like fewer children with measles.

manas.q: What does effectiveness mean in the 3Es?

children.note: Inputs are what you spend (nurses, drugs). Outputs are what you do (vaccinations given). Outcomes are the result for people (less disease).
Learning by comparing yourself with others who do it better.
Comparing your processes and results with the best, inside or outside your business, then copying good practice.

manas.q: What is benchmarking?

children.note: Comparing branches of the same business, for example one supermarket branch's stock losses against another's.
Comparing with direct rivals, for example another hospital chain's bed occupancy. Data can be hard to get.
Comparing a process with a top firm in another industry, for example a SACCO copying an airline's booking system.
Copying is not leading, rivals may not share data, and what works elsewhere may not suit you.
Kenyan examples with KES figures. All numbers checked.

children.topic: ROI and RI: Westlands hospital division
children.note: Profit KES 18m, capital employed KES 120m, cost of capital 12%. ROI = 18 ÷ 120 = 15%. RI = 18 − (120 × 12%) = 18 − 14.4 = KES 3.6m.

children.topic: New MRI scanner: does ROI mislead?
children.note: Scanner costs KES 30m and adds KES 4.2m profit a year: project ROI 14%. Division ROI falls to 22.2 ÷ 150 = 14.8%, so the manager rejects it. But 14% beats the 12% cost of capital.
Project RI = 4.2 − (30 × 12%) = 4.2 − 3.6 = +KES 0.6m. Division RI rises from 3.6m to 4.2m. RI says accept: the right answer for the group.
Mombasa: profit 9m on 50m = ROI 18%, RI at 10% = 9 − 5 = KES 4m. Kisumu: 20m on 160m = ROI 12.5%, RI = 20 − 16 = KES 4m. Same RI, but Mombasa uses capital better.
Profit stays KES 4.8m a year. With vehicles at NBV KES 32m, ROI = 15%. Two years later NBV is KES 16m: ROI = 30%. Nothing improved; the vehicles just got older.
A pharmacy chain: NOPAT KES 25m, economic capital KES 150m, WACC 13%. EVA = 25 − (150 × 13%) = 25 − 19.5 = KES 5.5m of value added.
Financial: fare income per vehicle. Customer: complaints per 1,000 trips. Internal: on-time departures %. Learning: drivers trained in safe driving.
Economy: syringe boxes bought at KES 800 not the budgeted KES 1,000. Efficiency: 300 children per nurse (2,400 ÷ 8 nurses). Effectiveness: coverage 84% vs target 90%.
Where candidates lose easy marks.
RI uses accounting profit and a chosen rate. EVA adjusts profit and capital and uses the after-tax WACC.
To judge a manager, use controllable profit. Charges they cannot change are unfair to include.
Tie each measure to the business in the question and its strategy. Generic lists score little.
Efficiency is output per input. Effectiveness is whether the goal was reached.
Try each, then open the bubbles below it to check.

children.topic: Q1: ROI or RI for a project?
children.note: A division has profit KES 12m, capital KES 80m, cost of capital 11%. A project costs KES 10m and earns KES 1.4m a year. Should the manager accept?
Project return 14% beats the 11% cost of capital, so the group gains. An ROI-judged manager may reject it; RI points to accept.

children.topic: Q2: scorecard for a private hospital
children.note: Suggest one measure for each of the four perspectives.
Financial: revenue per bed. Customer: patient satisfaction score. Internal: casualty waiting time. Learning and growth: training hours per nurse.

children.topic: Q3: 3Es for a county water company
children.note: Give one economy, one efficiency and one effectiveness measure.
Economy: cost per metre of pipe bought vs budget. Efficiency: water connections per technician. Effectiveness: % of homes with clean water daily.
A branch manager is paid a bonus on annual profit only. Name two risks.
Cutting staff training and shop repairs to boost profit (short-termism). Delaying needed new equipment because it lowers ROI.

nodeData.note: Old costing spreads overheads using one measure, like labour or machine hours, and this can give wrong product costs. Activity-based costing (ABC) and newer methods such as target, life-cycle and throughput costing give managers truer costs for pricing and cost control.

children.note: Start here: what goes wrong when all overheads are spread on one basis. You met absorption costing in CA25; here we see its limits.
Traditional absorption costing puts all factory overheads in one pot and shares them out by labour or machine hours. It assumes every overhead grows with production volume.

manas.q: What is the main weakness of traditional absorption costing?

children.note: Modern factories use machines and computers, so overheads are a large part of cost while direct labour is small. A small error in sharing overheads now makes a big error in product cost.
Costs like machine set-ups, ordering materials and quality checks depend on how many batches or orders you run, not how many units you make.
High-volume products get too much overhead (overcosted) and low-volume, complex products get too little (undercosted). The small special orders look more profitable than they really are.

manas.q: Under absorption costing, which products tend to be undercosted?

children.note: Wrong costs lead to wrong prices: the business may cut prices on loss-making special items and overprice its best sellers, losing customers to rivals.
Topic 2 builds on Topic 1 (performance management and the balanced scorecard) and on CA25 overheads, marginal and absorption costing. Those are not retaught here.
ABC shares overheads according to the activities that cause them. Products that use more of an activity carry more of its cost.
A costing method that first collects overheads by activity, then charges each activity to products based on how much of it each product uses.

manas.q: What is activity-based costing?

children.note: A task that uses resources, for example setting up a machine, ordering timber, inspecting finished chairs or delivering to customers.

manas.q: What is an activity in ABC?

children.note: A bucket that collects all the overhead cost of one activity, such as all set-up costs for the year.

manas.q: What is a cost pool?

children.note: The factor that makes the cost of an activity go up or down, such as the number of set-ups, purchase orders or inspections.

manas.q: What is a cost driver?

children.note: Cost pool ÷ total number of the driver. Example: set-up pool KES 600,000 ÷ 30 set-ups = KES 20,000 per set-up.

manas.q: How is a cost driver rate calculated?

children.note: 1) Find the main activities. 2) Collect overheads into a cost pool for each. 3) Pick a cost driver for each. 4) Work out a rate per driver. 5) Charge products: driver units used × rate.

manas.q: List the steps in ABC.

children.note: Unit-level costs grow with each unit (power for machines). Batch-level grow with each batch (set-ups). Product-level support a product line (design). Facility-level keep the site going (rent, security).

manas.q: Name the four levels of the ABC cost hierarchy.

children.note: More accurate product costs, better pricing, shows what really causes overheads, and helps find products, customers or activities that lose money.
Costly and slow to set up and update, needs good data, still uses some arbitrary sharing for facility costs, and may be too much for a small business with few products.

manas.q: Give two limitations of ABC.

children.note: When overheads are large, products differ a lot in batch size and complexity, and the business makes many products or serves very different customers.
Mti Bora Ltd, a Thika furniture maker, makes chairs and tables. Total production overheads for the year are KES 2,000,000. We cost both products both ways.

Chairs: 2,000 units, materials KES 1,500, labour KES 600, 1 machine hour each. Tables: 500 units, materials KES 6,000, labour KES 1,800, 4 machine hours each. Selling prices: chair KES 3,000, table KES 11,000.
Machine hours: chairs 2,000 × 1 = 2,000; tables 500 × 4 = 2,000; total 4,000. Rate = 2,000,000 ÷ 4,000 = KES 500 per machine hour.
Machine running KES 800,000; set-ups KES 600,000; material ordering KES 360,000; quality inspection KES 240,000. Total = KES 2,000,000, the same overheads.
Machine hours: chairs 2,000, tables 2,000. Set-ups: chairs 10, tables 20. Purchase orders: chairs 12, tables 24. Inspections: chairs 20, tables 40.
800,000 + 1,200,000 = KES 2,000,000, equal to total overheads. Nothing lost or double-counted.
Chair: prime cost 2,100; absorption full cost 2,600; ABC full cost 2,500. Table: prime cost 7,800; absorption 9,800; ABC 10,200.
Chair: absorption 3,000 − 2,600 = KES 400; ABC 3,000 − 2,500 = KES 500. Table: absorption 11,000 − 9,800 = KES 1,200; ABC 11,000 − 10,200 = KES 800.
Absorption: 2,000 × 400 + 500 × 1,200 = KES 1,400,000. ABC: 2,000 × 500 + 500 × 800 = KES 1,400,000. ABC changes how profit is split, not the total.
Tables use many set-ups, orders and inspections for few units, so ABC gives them more cost. Their margin falls from about 10.9% to 7.3%. Mti Bora should review table prices or batch sizes.
Using ABC information to manage and improve activities, not just to cost products.
ABM uses activity costs and drivers to cut waste, improve processes and make better decisions about products and customers.

manas.q: What is activity-based management?

children.note: Value-added activities make the product better in the customer's eyes (cutting and polishing wood). Non-value-added ones do not (moving stock around, reworking faults) and should be reduced.

manas.q: What is a non-value-added activity?

children.note: To cut set-up cost, cut the number of set-ups, for example by bigger batches or quicker changeovers. Managing the driver manages the cost.
ABC can cost customers too. A Nairobi supermarket ordering small amounts daily with many deliveries may cost more to serve than a wholesaler ordering monthly.
Budget each activity from the expected number of drivers, for example 40 set-ups × KES 20,000 = KES 800,000 for next year.
ABM gives the activity measures (set-up time, rework rate) for the internal business process view you met in Topic 1.
Start from the price customers will pay, then design the product to be made at a cost that still gives the required profit.
Target cost = target selling price − required profit. Cost gap = estimated cost − target cost.

manas.q: What is the target cost formula?

children.note: 1) Find the market price. 2) Take off the required profit. 3) Estimate the current cost. 4) Close the gap by redesign, cheaper materials or better methods before production starts.
Mti Bora plans a chair that sells at KES 8,000 and wants a 25% margin on price. Target cost = 8,000 − 2,000 = KES 6,000. Estimated cost KES 6,800, so the cost gap is KES 800.
Use value engineering: remove features customers do not value, use fewer parts, buy timber in bulk, or simplify assembly.

manas.q: What is value engineering?

children.note: A Mombasa clinic can set a price per check-up that patients will pay and work back to the cost it must hit, though service costs are harder to pin down.
Count all costs of a product over its whole life, not just one year's production costs.
Life-cycle costing adds up every cost from research and design to launch, production, marketing and final shutdown, and compares it with lifetime revenue.

manas.q: What is life-cycle costing?

children.note: Development, introduction, growth, maturity and decline. Most costs are committed at the design stage even though they are spent later.

manas.q: Name the stages of the product life cycle.

children.note: Pwani Juice, a Mombasa processor, plans a 3-year drink: research 1.2m, launch 0.8m, variable cost KES 300 × 20,000 crates = 6.0m, fixed 1.0m × 3 = 3.0m, shutdown 0.2m. Total KES 11.2m.
KES 11,200,000 ÷ 20,000 crates = KES 560 per crate. At a price of KES 700 the line makes money over its life.
Normal accounts show research as a cost of the year it is spent, so a product can look great later while never paying back its start-up costs.
Focus on the bottleneck: the one resource that limits how much the business can make and sell.
The scarcest resource, such as one pasteuriser that every crate of juice must pass through. Lost time here is lost profit for the whole business.

manas.q: What is a bottleneck resource?

children.note: Sales minus materials (the only truly variable cost). Labour and all other costs are treated as fixed "factory costs".

manas.q: How is throughput defined?

children.note: TPAR = return per factory hour ÷ cost per factory hour. Return per hour = throughput per unit ÷ bottleneck hours per unit. Cost per hour = total factory costs ÷ bottleneck hours available.

manas.q: What is the throughput accounting ratio formula?

children.note: Above 1: the product earns more than it costs to run the factory. Below 1: it loses money. Rank products by return per bottleneck hour.

manas.q: What does a TPAR below 1 mean?

children.note: Factory costs KES 6,000,000 a year; pasteuriser 2,000 hours, so cost per hour = KES 3,000. Mango crate: price 1,200, materials 500, 10 minutes. Passion crate: price 1,500, materials 600, 15 minutes.
Mango: throughput 700 × 6 crates an hour = KES 4,200. Passion: 900 × 4 = KES 3,600.
Mango 4,200 ÷ 3,000 = 1.4. Passion 3,600 ÷ 3,000 = 1.2. Both worthwhile; make mango first.
Demand: mango 9,000 crates (1,500 hours), passion 4,000. Make all mango, then 500 hours ÷ 0.25 = 2,000 passion. Throughput 6.3m + 1.8m = 8.1m less factory costs 6.0m = KES 2.1m profit.
Raise prices, cut material costs, cut factory costs, or speed up the bottleneck (a second shift, a faster machine).
Throughput accounting comes from Eliyahu Goldratt's theory of constraints: find the bottleneck, use it fully, make everything else work at its pace, then widen it.
Kaizen, backflush (JIT) and environmental costing, in brief.
Small, steady cost cuts while a product is already in production, with ideas from staff on the shop floor. Target costing works at design; Kaizen works after launch.

manas.q: What is Kaizen costing?

children.note: Mti Bora aims to cut chair cost by 2% a year: KES 2,500 → 2,450 in year 1 → 2,401 in year 2, by reducing offcut waste and sanding time.
Buy and make only when a customer order needs it, so stocks are very low. Needs reliable suppliers and good quality.
Under JIT, skip the detailed work-in-progress records. Record costs at the end, working back from finished units at standard cost.

manas.q: What is backflush costing?

children.note: Buy materials: Dr Raw and in-process 900,000 / Cr Payables 900,000. On finishing 1,000 units at 900 + 500: Dr Finished goods 1,400,000 / Cr Raw and in-process 900,000, Cr Conversion costs 500,000.
Identifying costs linked to the environment, such as waste disposal, effluent treatment, permits and clean-up, which are often hidden in general overheads.
A juice processor pays for fruit waste removal and water treatment to meet NEMA rules. Charging these to the products that cause them, ABC-style, shows their true cost.
Where marks are usually lost.
Check that the overheads shared under ABC equal total overheads. If not, a driver or a rate is wrong.

children.topic: Rate per unit vs per batch
children.note: A set-up cost is per batch. Charge the batch cost to the product, then divide by its units. Do not multiply the set-up rate by units.
No. In throughput accounting only materials are deducted; labour is part of factory costs.
Target costing sets the cost before production; Kaizen keeps cutting it after production starts.
ABC moves overheads between products. Total profit is the same unless the business acts on the new information.
For "discuss" questions, say why it matters to this business and give a reasoned recommendation.
Try each one, then open the steps.
Set-up costs are KES 300,000 and there are 50 set-ups. Product X uses 8 set-ups and makes 1,000 units. Find X's set-up cost per unit.
Price KES 2,000, materials KES 800, 0.5 bottleneck hours per unit. Factory costs KES 4,800,000; 4,000 bottleneck hours.
Throughput per unit = 2,000 − 800 = KES 1,200. Return per hour = 1,200 ÷ 0.5 = KES 2,400.
Cost per hour = 4,800,000 ÷ 4,000 = KES 1,200. TPAR = 2,400 ÷ 1,200 = 2.0, so the product is worth making.
A new bookshelf will sell for KES 5,000. The company wants 20% profit on price. Estimated cost is KES 4,300.
Profit = 20% × 5,000 = 1,000. Target cost = 5,000 − 1,000 = KES 4,000. Cost gap = 4,300 − 4,000 = KES 300 to remove.

nodeData.note: A transfer price is the price one part of a company charges another part for goods or services. It decides how profit is shared between divisions, and across borders it decides which country taxes the profit.

children.topic: What it is and why it matters
children.note: Start here: big businesses are split into divisions that trade with each other.
One division sells to another division of the same company or group. The price charged is the transfer price.

manas.q: What is a transfer price?

children.topic: Kenyan example: tea estate to packer
children.note: A Kericho tea estate grows and makes tea. Its own packing division in Nairobi packs it into boxes for supermarkets. The estate "sells" the tea to the packer.
The selling (supplying) division wants a high price. The buying (receiving) division wants a low price. Head office wants what is best for the whole group.

manas.q: Who wants a high and who wants a low transfer price?

children.note: The price is income for one division and a cost for the other. It moves profit between them, so it changes how good each manager looks.
Inside one country and before tax, the transfer price only moves profit from one pocket to another. Group profit stays the same.

manas.q: Does a transfer price change group profit (before tax)?

children.note: A badly set price can make a manager turn down work that is good for the group, or buy outside when buying inside is cheaper.
When divisions are in different countries, the price decides which country gets the profit to tax. Tax authorities like KRA watch this closely.

Builds on Topic 1 (performance management and the balanced scorecard: ROI, RI, divisional measures) and Topic 2 (activity-based and modern costing: what things really cost), and on CA25 Management Accounting.

children.topic: What a good transfer price does
children.note: Three aims. A good price meets all three; most real prices are a trade-off.
Managers acting for their own division also do what is best for the whole group. Their goals and the group goals point the same way.

manas.q: What is goal congruence in transfer pricing?

children.note: Each division's profit should be a fair picture of how well its manager did, so ROI and RI comparisons make sense.

manas.q: Why does a transfer price affect performance evaluation?

children.note: Managers are free to decide: buy inside or outside, sell inside or outside. Head office does not force the deal.

manas.q: What is divisional autonomy?

children.note: Managers who feel the price is fair work harder. A price that always makes one division look bad demotivates its staff.
The price gives a value to record internal sales and purchases in each division's accounts.
If head office imposes a price to get goal congruence, autonomy is lost. If managers are free, they may pick a price that hurts the group.
Three families: based on the market, based on cost, or agreed between managers.
Use the price the goods sell for outside, e.g. the tea auction price. Fair to both sides and good for evaluation when a real market exists.

manas.q: When is market price the best transfer price?

children.note: Market price less costs saved by selling inside, such as broker fees, delivery or bad debts. Shares the saving fairly.
There may be no outside market, or the market price may be a short-term dip. Products may also differ from what is sold outside.
Variable cost plus a share of fixed costs. The selling division only breaks even, so it earns no profit and has no reason to sell inside.

manas.q: What is the main weakness of a full cost transfer price?

children.note: Only the extra cost of one more unit. Good for group decisions when there is spare capacity, but the seller makes a loss equal to its fixed costs.

manas.q: What is a variable cost transfer price and its weakness?

children.note: Cost plus a mark-up, e.g. full cost + 20%. Gives the seller a profit, but the mark-up is a guess and may push the price too high.

manas.q: What is a cost-plus transfer price?

children.note: Charge at budgeted (standard) cost. Otherwise the seller passes its waste and inefficiency on to the buyer.

manas.q: Why use standard cost rather than actual cost?

children.note: Units are charged at variable cost, plus a fixed yearly fee to cover the seller's fixed costs and a profit. Buyer decides on true extra cost.

manas.q: What is a two-part tariff transfer price?

children.note: The seller records one price (e.g. market) and the buyer records another (e.g. variable cost). Head office removes the difference on consolidation.

manas.q: What is dual pricing?

children.note: Managers bargain and agree the price. Keeps autonomy, but takes time and the stronger negotiator may win, not the better division.

manas.q: What is a negotiated transfer price?

children.note: Head office simply sets the price. Quick and can ensure the right decision, but it reduces autonomy and motivation.
The one rule that answers most exam questions: find the range where both divisions are happy.
The seller needs at least its marginal (extra) cost plus any contribution it gives up by selling inside instead of outside.

manas.q: What is the minimum transfer price?

children.note: The contribution lost on the next best use of the capacity or scarce resource. It is zero when there is spare capacity.

manas.q: What is opportunity cost in the minimum transfer price?

children.note: The seller loses no outside sales, so minimum = marginal cost.

manas.q: What is the minimum transfer price with spare capacity?

children.note: Every unit sold inside is a lost outside sale. Minimum = marginal cost + lost contribution, which is the outside price less any costs saved.

manas.q: What is the minimum transfer price at full capacity?

children.note: If a resource like machine hours is short, add the contribution per hour of the best other product times the hours used.
The buyer pays no more than the lower of the outside purchase price and its net marginal revenue (selling price less its own extra costs).

manas.q: What is the maximum transfer price?

children.note: Any price between minimum and maximum makes both managers willing to trade and keeps the group better off.

manas.q: What is the profitable range for a transfer price?

children.note: No price works, and the group is better off if the units are not transferred. Each division should deal outside.
Chai Bora Group (made-up) has a Kericho tea estate division and a Nairobi packing division. Market prices are illustrative.
Estate: variable cost KES 180/kg, fixed costs KES 9m a year, capacity 200,000 kg. Packer buys 150,000 kg, adds packing cost KES 120/kg and fixed costs KES 6m, sells at KES 550/kg.
Made tea sells at the auction for KES 300/kg. The packer could also buy there at KES 300/kg.
The estate has spare capacity, so it loses no outside sales.
Marginal cost KES 180 + opportunity cost 0 = KES 180/kg.
Lower of auction price KES 300 and net marginal revenue 550 − 120 = KES 430. So KES 300/kg.
Any price from KES 180 to KES 300 per kg works for both divisions.
Now the estate can sell all it makes at the auction, but broker fees of KES 10/kg are saved on internal sales.
Lost contribution = 300 − 10 − 180 = KES 110. Minimum = 180 + 110 = KES 290/kg.
KES 290 to KES 300 per kg. A narrow range: close to the market price.
Profit for each division on 150,000 kg, KES.

Sales 150,000 × 550 = 82.5m. Less tea 37.5m, packing 18m, fixed 6m. Profit KES 21m.
Same tea, higher transfer price.
Sales 45m − 27m − 9m = KES 9m.
9m + 13.5m = KES 22.5m. Profit just moved KES 7.5m from packer to estate.
Full cost = 180 + (9m ÷ 150,000 = 60) = KES 240. Estate profit 0, packer KES 22.5m. Full cost + 20% = KES 288: estate 7.2m, packer 15.3m. Group still 22.5m.
Tea at KES 180/kg (27m) plus a yearly fee of KES 10.5m. Estate profit 37.5m − 36m = KES 1.5m, the same as a KES 250 price.
Estate records KES 300 (profit 9m). Packer records KES 180 (profit 31.5m). Total 40.5m; head office removes 150,000 × 120 = 18m. Group 22.5m.
A supermarket offers KES 340/kg for 20,000 kg extra packed tea. Both divisions have spare capacity. Transfer price is KES 300.
Its cost is 300 + 120 = KES 420/kg, above 340. It would lose KES 80/kg.
True extra cost is 180 + 120 = KES 300/kg. Gain 40 × 20,000 = KES 800,000. The price broke goal congruence.
Briefly: when the divisions are in different countries, the price moves taxable profit between countries.
A Kenyan subsidiary buys parts, brands or services from its foreign parent. The price it pays decides how much profit stays in Kenya.
Related companies must price as if they were strangers bargaining freely. The price should match what independent parties would agree.

manas.q: What is the arm's length principle?

children.note: The OECD guidelines for multinational enterprises and tax administrations are the main world reference. Most countries, Kenya included, follow them in broad terms.

manas.q: Which international guidelines govern transfer pricing for tax?

children.note: If a non-resident deals with a related Kenyan resident and the Kenyan side makes no or too little profit, KRA treats its profit as what arm's length parties would have made. Source: Income Tax Act Cap. 470, read 10 Nov 2026.

manas.q: What does section 18(3) of Kenya's Income Tax Act do?

children.note: The same arm's length rule applies to dealings with a preferential tax regime, e.g. a place taxing income below 20% or with no information exchange. (Checked 10 Nov 2026.)
Groups with consolidated turnover of KES 95 billion or more file a country-by-country report within 12 months after year end (ITA s.18C/18D). Check the current KRA rule; checked 10 Nov 2026.

manas.q: What is Kenya's country-by-country reporting threshold?

children.note: Such groups also keep a master file and local file, due within 6 months after year end. Kenyan entities must tell KRA who the ultimate parent is. (Checked 10 Nov 2026.)

Kenyan subsidiary sells cars for KES 500m, other costs 100m. Parent supplies parts costing it 200m. Parent country tax 10% (illustrative); Kenya 30% (check the current KRA rate; checked 10 Nov 2026). Figures KES m.
Kenya profit 500 − 250 − 100 = 150, tax 45. Parent profit 50, tax 5. Total tax 50; group profit 200.
Kenya profit 50, tax 15. Parent profit 150, tax 15. Total tax 30; group profit still 200.
Group pre-tax profit is the same, but tax falls by KES 20m and Kenya loses KES 30m of tax. That is profit shifting.
Shifted profit is lost tax for Kenya's roads, schools and hospitals. Under s.18(3) KRA can reset the price to KES 250m and collect the extra KES 30m.

manas.q: Why does KRA care about transfer prices?

children.note: Under the Tax Procedures Act, a scheme designed to avoid tax can be ignored, and the tax avoidance penalty is double the tax avoided (s.18A, s.85). Checked 10 Nov 2026.
Resident company corporation tax in Kenya is 30% (check the current KRA rate; checked 10 Nov 2026). Other countries' rates in examples here are illustrative.
Where marks are usually lost.
Before tax, internal prices only move profit. Group profit changes only if the price changes a decision (what is made, bought or sold).
At full capacity, a minimum of just marginal cost is wrong. Add the contribution lost on outside sales.
Fixed costs do not change with one more unit. Treating them as extra cost makes the buyer turn down good work.
The buyer's maximum is the lower of the outside price and net marginal revenue, not the higher one.
Broker fees, delivery or bad debts saved on internal sales reduce the minimum price.
Management prices aim at goal congruence. Tax prices must be arm's length. One group may need both views.

Component X: variable cost KES 200, needs 2 machine hours. Hours are scarce; the best other product earns KES 150 contribution per hour.
Minimum = 200 + (2 × 150) = KES 500 per unit.
In the Chai Bora example the price rises from KES 250 to KES 300. What happens to group profit?
Estate gains 7.5m, packer loses 7.5m. Group profit stays KES 22.5m because nothing else changed.

nodeData.note: International tax is about money that crosses borders: who gets to tax it, how much is held back at the border, and how to stop the same profit being taxed twice or not at all. This topic gives the Kenyan rules a CPA Advanced candidate and a working accountant need.

children.topic: What it is and why it matters
children.note: Start here: why cross-border deals need their own tax rules.
A Kenyan firm pays a UK consultant, a foreign bank lends to a Nairobi factory, a streaming app sells to Kenyan users. Each deal touches two tax systems.
The country where the earner lives and the country where the money is earned may both want to tax it. That is double taxation (taxed twice on the same income).

children.topic: The other risk: no tax at all
children.note: Groups can move profits to places with little or no tax using prices, loans and royalties inside the group. Rules on transfer pricing and interest stop this.
Mostly in the Income Tax Act Cap. 470 (rates, withholding, transfer pricing, DTAs) and the Tax Procedures Act 2015 (anti-avoidance, penalties, rulings).
You already know income tax, PAYE, corporation tax, capital allowances, VAT and tax procedures from CA26. Here we only add the cross-border layer on top.

children.topic: Who Kenya taxes: residence and source
children.note: Two questions decide it: where does the person belong, and where was the money earned?

children.topic: Source: where the income is earned
children.note: The source rule looks at where the work, asset or business that produced the income is. Kenya mainly taxes income that arises in or comes from Kenya.

manas.q: What does the source principle mean?

children.note: Residence links a person or company to a country. Being Kenyan resident brings resident rates and the right to claim relief for foreign tax under a DTA.

manas.q: What does the residence principle mean?

children.note: In simple terms, a company is Kenyan resident if it is set up (incorporated) in Kenya, or if its management and control is exercised in Kenya.
The Kenyan payer deducts withholding tax from what it pays. For most such payments that deduction is the end of the matter for the non-resident.
If the non-resident has a permanent establishment (a branch) here, the branch profits are taxed in Kenya through a tax return, much like a local company.

children.topic: Doing business here: PE, branch or subsidiary
children.note: A foreign company can trade in Kenya through a branch (a PE) or set up a Kenyan company (a subsidiary).
A fixed place in Kenya through which a foreign business carries on its work, such as an office, branch, factory, workshop or long building site.

manas.q: What is a permanent establishment?

children.topic: An agent can create a PE too
children.note: Even without an office, someone in Kenya who regularly signs contracts for the foreign company can make it have a PE. Treaties set the exact tests.
A non-resident company with a PE (branch) in Kenya pays 30% on branch profits from year of income 2024. Before that it was 37.5%. (check the current KRA rate; checked 10 Nov 2026)

manas.q: What is the corporation tax rate on a Kenyan branch of a non-resident company?

children.note: When working out branch profit (s.18(5)), ignore interest, royalties and management or professional fees "paid" to its own head office, and FX gains or losses on head-office balances.

manas.q: Which head-office charges are ignored when computing a PE profit?

children.note: A subsidiary is a separate resident company. It pays the resident rate of 30%, and dividends it sends to a foreign parent suffer 15% withholding tax. (check the current KRA rate; checked 10 Nov 2026)

children.topic: Branch or subsidiary? How to choose
children.note: Since 2024 both pay 30% on profit. The subsidiary adds dividend WHT when it pays out, but it limits the parent's legal risk. A treaty may change the dividend rate.
The Kenyan payer holds back part of the payment and pays it to KRA. The rate depends on what the payment is for.
Work out the tax on the GROSS amount, pay the non-resident the rest, and pay the tax over to KRA. The payer is liable if it forgets to deduct.

children.topic: A DTA may cut the rate
children.note: If the receiver lives in a country that has a tax treaty with Kenya, the treaty may set a lower rate. Check the treaty itself; this map does not list treaty rates.
How Kenya stops the same income being taxed twice, and how it stops people abusing treaties.
A treaty between two countries that shares out taxing rights and lowers or removes double tax. The Act calls them "special arrangements".

manas.q: What is a double taxation agreement (DTA)?

children.note: Where a valid DTA and the Income Tax Act say different things, the DTA wins for the people it covers.

manas.q: Which wins when a DTA and the Income Tax Act conflict?

children.note: A treaty company is denied the benefit if 50% or more of its owners (underlying ownership) are not residents of that treaty country, unless it is listed on that country's stock exchange.

manas.q: When does Kenya deny DTA benefits under the anti-treaty-shopping rule?

children.note: Where a DTA applies, a Kenyan resident taxed abroad gets a credit against Kenyan tax. The credit is the LOWER of the Kenyan tax and the foreign tax on that income.

manas.q: How is the foreign tax credit under a DTA measured?

children.note: Countries relieve double tax either by giving a credit for foreign tax paid, or by simply exempting the foreign income. Kenya's s.42 is a credit method.
A taxpayer can ask KRA for a written private ruling on how the law treats a planned deal. KRA may refuse if an anti-avoidance rule is involved.

children.note: Under s.85 of the Tax Procedures Act, the penalty for tax avoidance is twice the tax that would have been avoided.

children.note: Covered groups also keep a master file (the whole group) and a local file (the Kenyan entity), due within 6 months after year end.

children.note: New rules for income earned online and for very large groups paying too little tax.

children.note: If the service is supplied through a Kenyan permanent establishment, SEP tax does not apply; the branch is taxed on its profits instead.

manas.q: What is BEPS?

manas.q: Who is covered by Kenya's minimum top-up tax?

manas.q: How is the minimum top-up tax worked out?

children.note: Net income less 10% of employee costs and less 8% of the net book value of tangible assets. These carve-outs protect real jobs and real assets.

nodeData.note: Tax planning means arranging your business and personal affairs, within the law, so you pay the right tax and no more. This topic shows where the legal line is, the main planning ideas used in Kenya, and the risks of going too far.

children.topic: What it is and why it matters
children.note: Start here: three words that sound alike but sit on different sides of the law.
Using choices the law clearly gives you, such as claiming allowances or picking a business form, to lower tax. Fully legal and expected of a good adviser.

manas.q: What is tax planning?

children.note: Arranging affairs mainly to escape tax, often using the law in ways Parliament did not intend. Not a crime, but KRA can cancel the benefit and charge a penalty.

manas.q: What is tax avoidance?

children.note: Breaking the law to pay less: hiding sales, fake invoices, false expense claims or not filing. It is a crime and can lead to fines and prison.

manas.q: What is tax evasion?

children.note: Planning and avoidance are both legal acts; evasion is not. The grey area is avoidance: legal steps, but KRA can undo them and punish the taxpayer.

manas.q: Which of planning, avoidance and evasion is illegal?

children.note: If every fact is true and disclosed, you are planning or avoiding. If a fact is false or hidden from KRA, it is evasion.
Clients expect you to save them tax. You must do it without breaking the law, without harming your name and without ending up in a KRA dispute.

children.topic: The law on avoidance in Kenya
children.note: The Tax Procedures Act (TPA) 2015 gives KRA strong tools against avoidance.
The Act defines tax avoidance as a deal or scheme designed to avoid having to pay tax under any tax law. The key word is "designed": the purpose matters.

manas.q: How does TPA s.3 describe tax avoidance?

children.note: If the Commissioner finds a scheme entered into to get a tax benefit, KRA may work out the tax as if the scheme never happened. This is called a GAAR.

manas.q: What does the GAAR in TPA s.18A allow KRA to do?

children.note: The penalty for tax avoidance is double the tax that would have been avoided. This is on top of the tax itself.

manas.q: What is the tax avoidance penalty under TPA s.85?

children.note: The Income Tax Act also has targeted rules, such as transfer pricing (s.18(3)) and the limit on interest paid to non-residents (s.16(2)(j)).
Before a big deal, a taxpayer can ask KRA in writing how the law applies to it. KRA may refuse where an avoidance rule is involved.

manas.q: What is a private ruling?

children.note: Your duty is to the law and the profession, not only to the client.
ICPAK members follow a code of ethics based on the IESBA International Code of Ethics for Professional Accountants. Read them on the ICPAK and IESBA sites.

manas.q: Which ethics codes guide Kenyan accountants on tax work?

children.note: Integrity, objectivity, professional competence and due care, confidentiality, and professional behaviour. Tax advice must respect all five.

manas.q: What are the five fundamental ethical principles?

children.note: Explain the law and the risks, refuse to take part and record your advice. If they insist, you may have to stop acting for them.
Even if a scheme may be legal, ask if it would embarrass you in the news. Your reputation and ICPAK membership are on the line.
Tell the client to correct the error with KRA. Do not keep acting on a return you know is wrong.

When you buy an asset decides when you get the allowance.

manas.q: What are the investment allowance rates for machinery, computers and furniture?

Buying just before the year end brings the allowance a full year earlier. The tax saving comes sooner, which helps cash flow.
Special zones pay lower corporation tax for set periods, if conditions are met.
Corporation tax 10% for the first 10 years, then 15% for the next 10. (check the current KRA rate; checked 10 Nov 2026)

manas.q: What corporation tax rates apply to an SEZ enterprise?

children.note: 0% for the first 10 years, then 25%. (check the current KRA rate; checked 10 Nov 2026)

children.note: A company certified by the Nairobi International Financial Centre can pay 15% for its first 10 years, if conditions are met. (check the current KRA rate; checked 10 Nov 2026)
Pay staff in a way that is fair and tax-wise.
Most benefits (car, housing, school fees) count as pay and go through PAYE. Planning cannot make a taxable benefit disappear.

children.topic: Look for reliefs the law gives
children.note: Some items are exempt or deductible within limits, such as approved pension contributions. Check the current limits in the Income Tax Act first.
How a company is funded changes its tax bill.
Interest on business loans reduces taxable profit. Dividends to shareholders do not, so debt is usually cheaper after tax.

manas.q: Why is debt often more tax-efficient than equity?

A tax saving is worth nothing if it costs more later.
KRA can review returns, ask for records and raise an assessment. A weak scheme brings tax, the s.85 penalty and interest.
Customers, banks and the media judge firms that dodge tax. A legal scheme can still hurt the brand.

nodeData.note: How auditors check the accounts of a whole group of companies under ISA 600 (Revised), with a Nairobi parent and its Uganda and Tanzania subsidiaries as the example.

children.note: A group audit is the audit of consolidated accounts: the parent and its subsidiaries shown as one business. It builds on CA24 (what an audit is) and CA23 (group accounts).
One set of accounts that adds together the parent and the companies it controls, as if they were a single business.

manas.q: What are group financial statements?

children.topic: Why it is harder than one audit
children.note: The figures come from many companies, often in different countries, currencies, systems and with different auditors. Errors can hide in the joins between them.
ISA 600 (Revised) covers audits of group accounts, including using other auditors' work. It applies to periods beginning on or after 15 December 2023.

manas.q: Which standard covers group audits, and from when does the revised version apply?

children.note: The revised standard asks for a risk-based approach, more professional skepticism, better two-way talk with component auditors and clearer documentation. It links to ISQM 1, ISA 220 (Revised) and ISA 315 (Revised 2019).

Imagine Simba Holdings Ltd in Nairobi (the parent) owns Simba Uganda Ltd in Kampala and Simba Tanzania Ltd in Dar es Salaam. A Nairobi firm signs the group opinion; local firms audit the two subsidiaries. We use this group all through the map.
Learn who is who before learning the steps. Exam questions often test these words.
A part of the group, chosen by the group auditor, for which audit work may be done: a subsidiary, a branch, a division, or a shared service centre.

manas.q: What is a component in a group audit?

children.note: The partner who signs the auditor's report on the group accounts and takes full responsibility for the group audit, including how it is directed, supervised and reviewed.

manas.q: Who is the group engagement partner?

children.note: The partner and staff, including component auditors, who carry out the group audit. Its 'group auditor' part plans the work and draws the overall conclusion.

manas.q: Who is in the group engagement team?

children.note: An auditor who does work on a component's financial information for the group audit. They may be in the same firm, a network firm, or a different firm.

manas.q: What is a component auditor?

children.note: The people responsible for preparing the group accounts, usually the parent's directors and finance team who run the consolidation.
The group's board and audit committee. The group auditor tells them about the planned work, problems found and any concerns about component auditors.
The group auditor first understands the group, then decides where the risks are and what work to do, and who will do it.
Before saying yes, the partner checks they can get enough evidence: access to people and records across the group, and enough competent auditors.

manas.q: What must the group engagement partner be satisfied about before accepting a group audit?

children.topic: Understand the group and its environment
children.note: Learn the group structure, businesses, controls, IT systems and how consolidation is done. This follows the ISA 315 (Revised 2019) risk method you met in CA24.
Find out how figures flow from each company to the group accounts: reporting packs, group accounting policies, currency translation and eliminations.

manas.q: What does the group auditor need to understand about consolidation?

children.note: The revised standard drops the old 'significant component' size test. The group auditor decides where work is needed by looking at risks of material misstatement in the group accounts.

manas.q: How does ISA 600 (Revised) decide which components get audit work?

children.topic: Types of work at a component
children.note: Options include a full audit of the component's information, audit of chosen balances or transactions, or specific procedures on a risk. Work can be done by the group team or the component auditor.
Controls that cover the whole group, such as a shared IT system or a central treasury. Testing these once can give evidence for many components.
ISQM 1 sets the firm's quality system; ISA 220 (Revised) puts the partner in charge of quality on the engagement, including work by component auditors.
If another auditor does part of the work, the group auditor must know them, guide them and check their work.
Check that they are ethical and independent, competent, and work under good audit oversight. If not, the group team does the work itself.

manas.q: What must the group auditor understand about a component auditor?

children.note: Component auditors must follow the ethical rules for the group audit, such as the IESBA Code adopted by ICPAK, including independence from the group.
Clear written instructions: the work to do, component performance materiality, the reporting threshold, known risks, related parties to watch, and deadlines.

manas.q: What should group instructions to a component auditor include?

children.note: Talk both ways throughout the audit, not only at the end. The component auditor reports findings, misstatements, control weaknesses and any fraud or non-compliance.
The group auditor decides how much of the component auditor's documentation to review, based on risk. Review is deeper for high-risk areas and judgements.

manas.q: How does the group auditor evaluate a component auditor's work?

children.note: For higher risk, the group team may visit, attend meetings with component management, or review key working papers itself.

children.topic: When their work is not enough
children.note: If evidence is not enough, the group auditor asks for more work, does extra procedures itself, or in the end considers a modified opinion.
Materiality is set for the group first, then lower amounts are given to components so small errors cannot add up unseen.
Materiality for the group accounts as a whole, set by the group auditor using a benchmark such as profit before tax.

manas.q: What is group materiality?

children.note: A lower amount than group materiality, used to plan work so that missed and uncorrected errors together stay below materiality.
Set by the group auditor for each component where work is done. It must be lower than group performance materiality.

manas.q: How must component performance materiality compare with group performance materiality?

children.note: The risk that small errors in several components, each below their own limit, add up to a material error in the group accounts.

manas.q: What is aggregation risk?

children.note: An amount below which errors are too small to matter even when added up. Component auditors report every error above it to the group auditor.

manas.q: What is the clearly trivial threshold used for in a group audit?

children.note: Many group errors arise when the companies are put together, not inside each company.

children.topic: Reporting packs agree to audited figures
children.note: Check each component's figures in the consolidation agree to the information that was audited or reviewed.
Check components use the group's policies, or that adjustments are made where they differ.

manas.q: Why check accounting policies across components?

children.note: Sales, balances and dividends between group companies must be removed. Agree both sides match and investigate any difference.

manas.q: What does the auditor check on intra-group balances?

children.note: Profit on goods sold inside the group and still unsold at year end must be removed from group profit and inventory (CA23 skill).
Uganda shillings and Tanzania shillings figures are translated into Kenya shillings under IAS 21. Check the rates used and the translation difference.
Recalculate goodwill and the NCI share using IFRS 3 and IFRS 10, and check goodwill is tested for impairment under IAS 36.
If a component's year end differs from the parent's, check adjustments are made for big events in the gap.
Group companies, directors and their families can deal with each other. Share the list of related parties with component auditors and check disclosures under IAS 24.

manas.q: How are related parties handled in a group audit?

children.note: Ask component auditors to report events after their work up to the group report date, and do group-level review of events too (ISA 560).

manas.q: How does the group auditor cover subsequent events at components?

children.note: Sometimes the group auditor cannot reach information. And the final report has special rules.
Access may be blocked by group management, by law in another country, or by events like war. The auditor tries other ways to get evidence first.

manas.q: What can the auditor do when access to a component is restricted?

children.note: If access is blocked and the effect could be material, the opinion may be qualified or a disclaimer given. Imposed by management at acceptance stage, the partner may decline.
In an unmodified opinion, the report must not mention component auditors. The group engagement partner takes full responsibility.

manas.q: Can an unmodified group audit report refer to a component auditor?

children.note: Only if law requires it, or to explain a modified opinion, and then the report says this does not reduce the group auditor's responsibility.
Tell the board about the scope, planned involvement in component auditors' work, concerns about their quality, limits on access and any fraud found.
Record the risk assessment, which components got which work, the involvement in component auditors' work, and key communications.
Numbers are made up for learning. Benchmark percentages are illustrative only — firm methodology decides.
Group profit before tax KES 800 million. Illustrative benchmark 5% gives group materiality KES 40 million (800m × 5%). Illustrative — firm methodology decides.
Illustrative 75% of KES 40m = KES 30 million. This is used to plan the group work.
Set below KES 30m: Uganda KES 18 million, Tanzania KES 15 million. Each is lower than group performance materiality, as required.
Illustrative 5% of KES 40m = KES 2 million. Uganda and Tanzania auditors report every error above KES 2m.
Uncorrected errors: Parent KES 10m, Uganda KES 14m (below its KES 18m limit), Tanzania KES 12m (below its KES 15m limit).
10 + 14 + 12 = KES 36 million. Each looked small alone, but together they are close to group materiality of KES 40m.
KES 36m is above performance materiality of KES 30m, so ask management to correct some errors or do more testing before signing.
Parent sold goods to Simba Tanzania for KES 60m; they cost the parent KES 45m. 40% of the goods are still in Tanzania's stock at year end.
Dr Group revenue KES 60m / Cr Group cost of sales KES 60m. Group sales and purchases both fall, profit unchanged.
Profit = 60 − 45 = KES 15m. Unsold 40% × 15m = KES 6m. Dr Group cost of sales KES 6m / Cr Group inventory KES 6m.
Recompute the KES 6m, confirm the 40% to Tanzania's stock count, and check the entries are in the consolidation.
Parent shows KES 25m owed by Simba Tanzania. Tanzania shows only KES 22m owed to the parent.
25 − 22 = KES 3m. Common causes: cash or goods in transit at year end, or exchange rate differences.
Trace to bank statements and delivery notes after year end. If it is cash in transit: Dr Cash in transit KES 3m / Cr Intra-group receivable KES 3m, then both balances (22m) cancel.
Points that lose easy marks.
The revised standard scopes work by risk, not just by size. Use risk-based language in answers.

children.topic: Component limit equal to group limit
children.note: Component performance materiality must be below group performance materiality, or aggregation risk is not covered.
Do not mention them in an unmodified report. The group partner owns the whole opinion.
Testing each company is not enough; eliminations, translation and goodwill must be audited too.
Communication with component auditors must be two-way and ongoing, from planning to completion.
Try each question, then open the steps.
Group PBT is KES 800m. Using illustrative 5% and 75%, set group materiality, performance materiality and a suitable component limit.
Group materiality = 5% × 800m = KES 40m (illustrative — firm methodology decides).
Group performance materiality = 75% × 40m = KES 30m.
Give each component a lower figure, e.g. Uganda KES 18m, and explain this reduces aggregation risk.

children.topic: Q2: Uganda auditor is new to you
children.note: How should the group auditor decide whether to use the Uganda firm's work?
Check ethics and independence, competence and the regulatory oversight they work under.
Send clear instructions and agree two-way reporting dates.
Review their work based on risk; if not satisfied, do the work yourself.
Group management refuses access to Simba Tanzania records. Explain the effect.
Try other evidence, e.g. group-level records or the component's management accounts.
If evidence is still lacking and the effect may be material, qualify the opinion; if pervasive, disclaim.
Tell those charged with governance about the restriction.

nodeData.note: How an audit firm makes sure every audit it signs is done well. ISQM 1 sets up the firm-wide system, ISQM 2 covers engagement quality reviews, and ISA 220 (Revised) covers the partner on each audit.

children.topic: What it is and why it matters
children.note: Quality management is the set of habits, checks and people an audit firm uses so that its work is good every time, not just by luck.
Banks, investors, KRA and the public rely on audit reports. A poor audit can let fraud or big errors go unnoticed and destroy the firm's name.
The firm builds one system for all its work (ISQM 1). Each audit team then applies it on its own job (ISA 220 Revised).

manas.q: What are the two levels of quality management in an audit firm?

children.note: ISQM 1 covers the firm's system, ISQM 2 covers engagement quality reviews, and ISA 220 (Revised) covers quality on a single audit.

manas.q: Name the three IAASB standards on quality management and what each covers.

children.note: ISQM 1 replaced the older ISQC 1. Firms had to have their new systems designed and in place by 15 Dec 2022.

manas.q: Which standard did ISQM 1 replace, and by when did firms need their systems in place?

children.note: From CA24 you know ethics, risk and evidence. Group audits (topic 1) showed ISA 600 (Revised) is aligned with ISQM 1 and ISA 220 (Revised).
A risk-based system the firm tailors to its own size and clients. It is not a fixed checklist.
Set quality objectives, find what could stop you meeting them (quality risks), then design responses to those risks.

manas.q: What are the three steps of the ISQM 1 risk-based approach?

children.note: The results the firm wants to achieve, for example 'staff are competent' or 'we only accept clients we can serve well'.
Things that could reasonably happen and stop an objective being met. The firm judges how likely and how serious each one is.

manas.q: What is a quality risk under ISQM 1?

children.note: Policies and procedures that deal with a quality risk, such as a checklist, a training plan or a second review.
A two-partner firm in Nairobi needs a much simpler system than a large network firm. The aim is the same; the detail differs.

manas.q: Does ISQM 1 require the same system in a small and a large firm?

children.note: The system aims to give the firm reasonable (high, not absolute) assurance that it and its people meet standards and issue the right reports.
ISQM 1 groups the system into eight parts that work together.
Leaders set the tone: quality comes before fees, roles are clear and enough resources are given.

manas.q: What does the governance and leadership component cover?

children.note: The firm and its people follow ethics rules, including independence. In Kenya this means ICPAK's code, which is based on the IESBA Code.
Before taking or keeping a client, check integrity of the client, the firm's competence, time and ethics.

manas.q: What must a firm consider before accepting or continuing a client?

children.note: How audits are done: direction, supervision, review, consultation on hard issues and handling differences of opinion.
People, technology (audit software) and intellectual resources (methodology, guides). Includes outside service providers.
The right information reaches the right people at the right time, inside the firm and with outsiders like regulators.
The process for setting objectives, spotting quality risks and designing responses. It feeds all other parts.

manas.q: Which ISQM 1 component sets objectives and identifies quality risks?

children.note: Checking the system works (e.g. file inspections), finding deficiencies, their root causes, and fixing them.

manas.q: What is the monitoring and remediation component?

children.note: Think 'G-E-A-P-R-I-R-M': Governance, Ethics, Acceptance, Performance, Resources, Information, Risk process, Monitoring.
Who answers for the system, how weaknesses are found and fixed, and the yearly sign-off.
The firm's CEO or managing partner (or managing board) carries ultimate responsibility and accountability for the whole system.

manas.q: Who has ultimate responsibility for the firm's system of quality management?

children.note: Named people run day-to-day parts, like independence or monitoring. They need the right experience, time and authority.
A gap in the system: a missing objective, risk or response, or a response that does not work as planned.

manas.q: What is a deficiency under ISQM 1?

children.note: Judge how serious a deficiency is and how widely it spreads. Serious and widespread ones need urgent action.
The real reason behind a deficiency. Fix the cause, not just the symptom, or the problem comes back.

manas.q: Why must a firm look for the root cause of a deficiency?

children.note: Actions to fix the deficiency, then checking that the fix actually worked.
At least once a year, the person with ultimate responsibility evaluates the system and concludes whether it gives reasonable assurance.

manas.q: How often must the system of quality management be evaluated, and by whom?

children.note: The system meets its objectives; meets them except for some issues; or does not meet them. The last two need prompt action.
An extra, objective check on the big judgements in certain audits, done before the report is signed.
An objective look at the significant judgements the team made and the conclusions it reached, done before the report is dated.

manas.q: What is an engagement quality review?

children.note: ISQM 1 requires it for audits of listed entities, where law or regulation requires it, and where the firm decides it is needed for higher-risk work.

manas.q: Which engagements need an engagement quality review?

children.note: Someone with enough competence, time and authority who is objective and independent of the team. They are not part of the audit team.

manas.q: What makes a person eligible to be an engagement quality reviewer?

children.note: A partner who just led the audit should wait before reviewing that same client, so they are not checking their own decisions. ISQM 2 sets two years, or longer if ethics rules demand.

manas.q: What is the cooling-off idea in ISQM 2?

children.note: Reads key papers, discusses significant matters with the partner, checks significant judgements and that the partner was properly involved.
The engagement partner must not date the auditor's report until the reviewer says the review is complete.
The reviewer records what was reviewed, by whom and when, and that it was finished. This goes on the audit file.
For audits and reviews of periods beginning on or after 15 Dec 2022.
Quality on one audit. The engagement partner owns quality from start to finish.
The engagement partner takes overall responsibility for managing and achieving quality on the audit.

manas.q: Who is responsible for quality on an individual audit under ISA 220 (Revised)?

children.note: The partner must be involved enough throughout, not only at the end, to judge whether the work is right.
Tasks can be given to managers and seniors, but the partner still answers for the result.
The partner confirms the team understands and meets ethics rules and deals with any threats found.
The partner checks that the firm's acceptance procedures were followed for this client.
The partner makes sure the team has enough skilled people, time and tools for the job.
Plan and guide the team, watch progress, and review work, especially significant matters, before signing.

manas.q: What three things does the partner do with the team's work?

children.note: Hard issues are discussed with experts. Differences of opinion are settled under firm policy before the report is dated.
The partner encourages a questioning mind and watches for pressure, such as tight deadlines, that weakens it.
Ethics is one of ISQM 1's eight components, and it rests on the IESBA Code.
Integrity, objectivity, professional competence and due care, confidentiality, and professional behaviour.

manas.q: List the five fundamental principles of the IESBA Code.

children.note: Self-interest, self-review, advocacy, familiarity and intimidation.

manas.q: Name the five threats to compliance with the fundamental principles.

children.note: Actions that bring a threat down to an acceptable level, like using a separate team or an independent review.
Being, and being seen to be, free from influence by the client. Firms often get yearly written confirmations from staff.
Staying on one client too long creates familiarity. Rotation and cooling-off rules deal with this.
How quality is checked from outside the firm in Kenya.
ICPAK licenses practising accountants in Kenya and runs a practice review (quality assurance) programme for audit firms.
Reviewers visit firms, look at the firm-level system and inspect sample audit files against ISQM 1 and the ISAs.
A clean result, a list of matters to fix with a follow-up visit, or referral for discipline in serious cases.
Keep the ISQM 1 documents, annual evaluation, monitoring results and complete audit files ready to show.

Next year's inspection re-tests these files. If problems remain, the root cause was wrong and is looked at again.

No. Partner A would be checking their own earlier judgements. Cooling-off applies.

It is risk-based and tailored. Answers should link objective, risk and response.
Wrong. The reviewer is outside the team and must stay objective.
Retraining one person without asking why the problem arose misses the root cause.
The report cannot be dated before the EQ review is done and the partner has reviewed enough work.

The team lacks competence to audit bank loans and regulatory rules.
Hire or borrow a banking expert, train the team, and plan an EQ review for this audit.
Why is root cause analysis important in monitoring and remediation?
It finds why the deficiency happened, so the fix targets the real cause and stops the problem repeating.
