nodeData.note: Beyond the statutory audit, accountants check forecasts, controls, sustainability data and more. This map explains the levels of assurance, the main IAASB standards and the reports, with Kenyan examples.

children.topic: What assurance is and why it matters
children.note: Assurance means an independent expert checks information so that users can trust it more. A statutory audit is one kind; this topic covers the other kinds.
Someone (a bank, investor, regulator) relies on information prepared by someone else. An independent accountant checks it and says how far it can be trusted.

manas.q: What is an assurance engagement?

children.note: It reduces the risk of relying on wrong or biased information, for example a bank lending against a forecast or a customer relying on an outsourced payroll provider.
You met the statutory audit in CA24 Auditing and Assurance, and in this paper topics 1 Group audits and 2 Quality management. Here we apply the same thinking to other information.

ISAE 3000 (Revised) is the general IAASB standard for assurance on anything other than audits or reviews of past financial statements. Topic-specific ISAEs such as 3400, 3402 and 3410 sit on top of it.

manas.q: Which standard covers assurance other than audits or reviews of historical financial information?

children.note: Firms doing reviews and other assurance or related services must run a quality management system under ISQM 1, just as for audits.

children.topic: The five elements of an engagement
children.note: Every assurance engagement has five building blocks. If one is missing, it is not an assurance engagement.
Three parties: the practitioner (the checker), the responsible party (who prepares the information) and the intended users (who rely on it).

manas.q: Name the three parties in an assurance engagement.

children.note: The thing being checked: a forecast, a set of controls, a greenhouse gas statement, a loan schedule and so on. It must be identifiable and measurable.
The yardstick used to measure the subject matter, such as IFRS, a GHG protocol or a contract. Good criteria are relevant, complete, reliable, neutral and understandable.

manas.q: What makes criteria suitable?

children.note: Enough good-quality evidence to support the conclusion. How much depends on the level of assurance and the risk.
A written report giving the practitioner's conclusion to the intended users.
Three parties, Subject matter, Criteria, Evidence, Report. Use it to check any scenario in the exam.

manas.q: List the five elements of an assurance engagement.

children.note: Assurance comes in two levels and two engagement types. Getting these right is key to the whole topic.
A high (but not absolute) level of assurance. More work is done and the conclusion is positive: the information IS fairly stated. An audit is the usual example.

manas.q: What is reasonable assurance and how is its conclusion worded?

children.note: A meaningful but lower level. Less work, mostly enquiry and analytical review, and the conclusion is negative-form: nothing has come to our attention to suggest it is wrong.

manas.q: What is limited assurance and how is its conclusion worded?

children.note: Positive: 'in our opinion it is fairly presented'. Negative-form: 'we are not aware of anything showing it is not fairly presented'. Users must not read a negative-form conclusion as an opinion.

manas.q: Compare a positive and a negative-form conclusion.

children.note: Management measures the subject matter and prepares the information first; the practitioner then checks that information. Most engagements in this topic are this type.

manas.q: What is an attestation engagement?

children.note: The practitioner measures or evaluates the subject matter themselves and reports on it, for example directly assessing a control system with no management report.

manas.q: What is a direct engagement?

children.note: Agreed-upon procedures and compilations are related services. They give no assurance at all, even though an accountant's name is on the report.
Each type of engagement has its own IAASB standard. Learn what is checked, what level of assurance is given and what the report looks like.
A review gives limited assurance on financial statements, mostly through enquiry and analytical procedures.
Used when the practitioner is NOT the entity's auditor, for example a small company that is exempt from audit but whose bank wants some comfort.

manas.q: What does ISRE 2400 (Revised) cover?

children.note: Used when the entity's own auditor reviews interim (for example half-year) financial information. The auditor already knows the business well.

manas.q: What does ISRE 2410 cover?

children.note: Ask management and staff questions, compare figures with last year and budget, investigate unusual movements, read the statements against the framework.
Checking forecasts and projections, for example cash-flow forecasts that support a loan application.
A forecast uses management's best-estimate assumptions. A projection uses hypothetical 'what if' assumptions, for example a new wing that may not be built.

manas.q: What is the difference between a forecast and a projection?

children.note: Limited assurance on the assumptions (nothing suggests they are unreasonable) plus a positive opinion that the forecast is properly prepared on those assumptions and presented under the framework.

manas.q: What does an ISAE 3400 report conclude on?

children.note: The report warns that actual results are likely to differ, because future events often do not happen as expected.
Check the arithmetic, compare assumptions with past results and market data, check consistency with approved plans, and check the accounting policies match the actual statements.
Assurance on controls at an outsourced provider (for example a payroll bureau or IT host) so that client auditors can rely on it.
The service organisation, its customers (user entities) and the customers' auditors. One report saves every customer's auditor visiting the provider.
Covers the description of the system and whether controls are suitably designed and implemented at a single date. It says nothing about whether they worked over time.

manas.q: What does an ISAE 3402 Type 1 report cover?

children.note: Covers everything in Type 1 PLUS whether the controls operated effectively throughout a period, with the tests done and results. Auditors prefer Type 2.

manas.q: What does an ISAE 3402 Type 2 report add?

children.note: Assurance on climate and other sustainability information is growing fast in Kenya and worldwide.
Covers assurance on an entity's greenhouse gas emissions statement, at reasonable or limited assurance.

manas.q: Which standard covers assurance on greenhouse gas statements?

children.note: A stand-alone IAASB standard for sustainability assurance, issued November 2024. It covers any sustainability topic and framework, at limited or reasonable assurance, and can be used by accountants and non-accountants.

manas.q: What is ISSA 5000?

children.note: The IAASB adoption list (updated September 2026) shows ICPAK has adopted ISSA 5000, generally effective for periods beginning on or after 15 December 2026, with early use allowed (checked 11 Nov 2026).
The client and practitioner agree specific checks; the practitioner does them and reports the facts found.
The report lists each procedure and what was found. There is no opinion or conclusion, so users draw their own conclusions.

manas.q: What does an agreed-upon procedures report give?

children.note: Under the revised standard independence is not automatically required, but the report must say whether the practitioner is independent.
Procedures must be specific and give the same result whoever does them, for example 'agree each balance to the signed form', not 'check if loans are fine'.
The accountant uses accounting skill to collect, classify and summarise the client's data into financial information.
The practitioner does not verify the data. The report says clearly that no audit or review was done and no assurance is given.

manas.q: What assurance does a compilation under ISRS 4410 give?

children.note: A Nairobi duka owner asks an accountant to prepare annual accounts from the cash book and M-Pesa statements for a loan application.
An investigation of a business before a deal, such as buying a company or a large investment. Covers finances, tax, legal, commercial and operational risks.

manas.q: What is due diligence?

children.note: Investigating suspected fraud or disputes so that findings can stand up in court, for example tracing missing SACCO funds. Evidence handling must be careful and well documented.

manas.q: What is forensic accounting?

children.note: Two short cases with real numbers in KES. Check every figure yourself.

children.topic: Hospital forecast for a bank loan
children.note: A Kenyan private hospital wants a KES 120,000,000 bank loan for a new wing. The bank asks for an ISAE 3400 report on the year-1 profit forecast.
Outpatients 40,000 visits x KES 2,500 = KES 100,000,000. Inpatients 6,000 bed-days x KES 8,000 = KES 48,000,000. Total revenue KES 148,000,000 (arithmetic correct).
Staff KES 60,000,000 + drugs and supplies (30% of revenue) KES 44,400,000 + other running costs KES 18,000,000 + depreciation KES 12,000,000 = KES 134,400,000.
Revenue KES 148,000,000 - costs KES 134,400,000 = profit KES 13,600,000. The arithmetic adds up, but something is missing.
The bank's offer letter says 14% a year. Interest = 120,000,000 x 14% = KES 16,800,000. Corrected result: 13,600,000 - 16,800,000 = a LOSS of KES 3,200,000.
Last year's actual visits were 28,000. The forecast assumes 40,000, a rise of 12,000 or about 42.9%. Ask for evidence such as new specialists or insurer contracts.
Ask management to correct the interest. If the visits assumption cannot be supported, the conclusion on assumptions is modified or the practitioner withdraws.

children.topic: AUP findings table for a SACCO
children.note: A SACCO board asks for agreed-upon procedures: agree 10 member loan balances in the ledger to signed loan forms. The report lists facts only.
Eight of the ten loans selected agreed exactly with the signed loan forms. No exceptions on these.
Ledger KES 250,000; signed form KES 205,000. Difference KES 45,000 more in the ledger. Possibly a typing (transposition) error, but the report just states the facts.
Ledger KES 80,000; signed form KES 88,000. Difference KES 8,000 less in the ledger.
It states the procedures, the findings above, that no audit or review was done, that no assurance is given, and whether the practitioner is independent. The board decides what it means.
These errors cost marks again and again. Read each one slowly.
Agreed-upon procedures give NO assurance, only factual findings. Same for compilations.
Type 1 = design at a point in time. Type 2 = design plus operating effectiveness over a period. An auditor wanting to rely on controls needs Type 2.
A review under ISRE 2400 or 2410 gives a negative-form conclusion, never 'in our opinion ... true and fair'.

children.topic: Giving assurance on achieving a forecast
children.note: Under ISAE 3400 the practitioner never says the forecast WILL be achieved. They report on assumptions and preparation only.
If there are no suitable criteria or no intended users, it is not an assurance engagement. Test every scenario against 3-S-C-E-R.
Assurance work needs independence. For AUP, state whether you are independent. Remember the ISQM 1 system applies.
Try each question before opening the answer steps.

children.topic: Q1: A bank wants comfort fast
children.note: An unaudited company's bank asks for 'some comfort' on its financial statements at low cost. What engagement fits?
Financial statements, not audited, and the user accepts a lower level of comfort at lower cost.
A review under ISRE 2400 (Revised), because the practitioner is not the entity's auditor.
Limited assurance with a negative-form conclusion, based mainly on enquiry and analytical procedures.
A hospital forecast shows profit KES 13.6m but leaves out interest of 14% on a KES 120m loan. What do you report?
Interest 120m x 14% = 16.8m. Profit becomes 13.6m - 16.8m = loss of KES 3.2m.

children.topic: Step 2: ask management to fix it
children.note: The forecast is not properly prepared on its own assumptions while the interest is missing.
Modify the opinion on preparation (or withdraw). Never state the forecast will be achieved.
A bank's auditor wants to rely on the controls of an outsourced card-processing firm for the whole year. Which report?
An ISAE 3402 Type 2 report, because it tests whether the controls worked throughout the period, not just whether they were designed at one date.

children.topic: Why public sector accounting is different
children.note: Government spends taxpayers' money to give services, not to make profit. So its accounts must show that money was raised and spent lawfully, as the budget allowed, and to good effect.
A county hospital or a ward road is judged by the service it gives, not by profit. A 'surplus' only means income was more than costs; it is not the goal.

manas.q: What is the main aim of a public sector entity, and how is that different from a business?

children.note: Parliament or the county assembly approves the budget in an Appropriation Act. Spending beyond it, or on something else, is unlawful even if the money is in the bank.

manas.q: Why does the budget matter more in government than in a business?

children.note: Officials must show citizens, Parliament and the county assembly how public money was used. The Constitution asks for openness, public participation and clear financial reporting (Article 201).

Parliament and county assemblies, the Auditor-General, the Controller of Budget, the National Treasury, lenders, donors and ordinary citizens. They want to know: was money used lawfully, and what do we owe and own?

manas.q: Name four users of public sector financial statements.

children.note: A government has no shareholders. What is left after liabilities is called net assets/equity, not owners' capital.

manas.q: What is 'net assets/equity' in public sector accounts?

children.note: CA26 Public Finance and Taxation taught the Kenyan budget cycle and public finance. CA23 Financial Reporting taught IFRS. This topic joins them: IFRS-style accounts for government.
Worldwide, the IPSAS Board writes public sector standards. In Kenya, the Public Sector Accounting Standards Board (PSASB) decides which standards and formats public entities must use.
The International Public Sector Accounting Standards Board. It is an independent board supported by IFAC that issues IPSAS for governments and other public bodies.

manas.q: What is the IPSASB?

children.note: International Public Sector Accounting Standards. Most are based on IFRS and changed where government is different, e.g. taxes, grants and budgets.

manas.q: What are IPSAS and what are most of them based on?

children.note: Set up under the PFM Act (s.192–194). It sets accounting standards, minimum books of account, internal audit procedures and statement formats for all public entities.

manas.q: What does Kenya's PSASB do?

children.note: Act No. 27 of 2026 added: a framework for accrual accounting, a risk-management framework and sustainability reporting standards for public entities (checked 11 Nov 2026).
The Public Finance Management Act (Cap 412A) sets how public money is budgeted, spent, accounted for and reported. Financial year runs 1 July to 30 June.

manas.q: When does the Kenyan government financial year start and end?

children.note: Under PFM s.68 each accounting officer answers to the National Assembly for lawful, efficient and transparent use of resources, and must keep proper records.
Cash basis records money only when it comes in or goes out. Accrual basis records income when earned and costs when incurred, and shows assets and debts too.
A single IPSAS for governments not yet on accrual. It reports cash received, cash paid and cash balances, plus some extra disclosures.

manas.q: What does the cash basis IPSAS report?

children.note: The full set of IPSAS. Records revenue when earned, expenses when incurred, and shows all assets (roads, buildings) and liabilities (pending bills, pensions, debt).

manas.q: What does accrual accounting record that cash accounting misses?

children.note: Unpaid supplier bills, money owed to the county, the value and wear of roads and buildings, and pension promises. Accounts can look healthy while debts pile up.
Kenya used cash basis IPSAS since 2014. Cabinet approved accrual on 7 Mar 2024, gazetted 30 Aug 2024 (Notice 11033), effective 1 July 2024.

manas.q: When did accrual IPSAS take effect for Kenya's national and county governments?

links.title: National Treasury: cash to accrual press statement (3 Oct 2024)

children.note: For the year ending 30 June 2025, with a three-year transition, a steering committee, and revised IFMIS and Standard Chart of Accounts.

links.title: National Treasury: cash to accrual press statement (3 Oct 2024)

children.note: Pending bills, pensions, public debt, receivables, fixed assets and natural resources will now appear in the statements.

links.title: National Treasury: cash to accrual press statement (3 Oct 2024)

children.note: Gives reliefs when moving to accrual IPSAS, e.g. extra time to recognise some assets and liabilities. Kenya uses these reliefs in the first year.

manas.q: What does IPSAS 33 do?

links.title: National Treasury: cash to accrual press statement (3 Oct 2024)

children.note: Counting and valuing every road, clinic and vehicle, finding all unpaid bills, and training staff. That is why there is a transition period.
Under accrual IPSAS a public entity prepares a full set of statements, much like IFRS, plus a budget comparison. IPSAS 1 covers presentation.
What the entity owns (assets) and owes (liabilities) at year end; the difference is net assets/equity. Like a balance sheet.

manas.q: What does the statement of financial position show?

children.note: Revenue less expenses for the year gives a surplus or deficit. Like an income statement, but no 'profit'.

manas.q: What is the public sector version of the income statement called?

children.note: Shows how net assets moved: opening balance, surplus or deficit, revaluations and other changes, closing balance.
Cash from operating, investing and financing activities (IPSAS 2). Shows where cash came from and went.
Compares the approved and final budget with actual amounts, on the same basis as the budget, and explains big differences.

manas.q: What does IPSAS 24 require?

children.note: Explain the policies used and give detail behind the numbers, e.g. a list of pending bills by age.
Accounting officers prepare annual statements incl. appropriation accounts explaining variances, debt, assets and liabilities, and performance.

manas.q: What must annual statements under PFM s.81 include?

children.note: Submit to the Auditor-General within two months of year end (copies to CoB, Treasury, CRA), and publish. Older books say three; check the current rule, checked 11 Nov 2026.

manas.q: Within how long after year end must s.81 statements go to the Auditor-General?

children.note: Audits and reports within six months of year end (Constitution Art 229). Parliament or the county assembly debates the report.
The special accrual topics in government: money received for nothing in return, money given away, roads and buildings, and unpaid bills.
Exchange: you give roughly equal value back (hospital fees for treatment). Non-exchange: you get money without giving equal value back (taxes, grants, transfers).

manas.q: What is the difference between exchange and non-exchange transactions?

children.note: One revenue standard for government. It has two models, depending on whether there is a binding arrangement with the giver.

manas.q: What decides which IPSAS 47 revenue model applies?

children.note: There are enforceable obligations (e.g. a grant that must be spent on a clinic or returned). Revenue is recognised as those obligations are met; until then it is a liability.
No enforceable obligations, e.g. most taxes or a free equitable-share transfer. Revenue is recognised when the entity controls the resource.
Taxes are compulsory payments; transfers move money between governments (e.g. equitable share to counties); grants come from donors. All are usually non-exchange.
Covers giving resources without getting anything directly back, e.g. bursaries or grants to schools. Kenya effective 1 July 2026 (IPSASB: 1 Jan 2026).

manas.q: What does IPSAS 48 cover and when is it effective in Kenya?

children.note: Leases (IPSAS 43), service concessions (IPSAS 32), employee benefits (IPSAS 39), financial instruments (IPSAS 41) and social benefits (IPSAS 42).
IPSAS 45 is the current PPE standard. Record assets at cost (or value), then depreciate them over their useful life.
Roads, bridges, water pipes and power lines. Long-lived and often hard to value; recorded as PPE and depreciated, usually part by part.

manas.q: Give three examples of infrastructure assets.

children.note: Goods or services received but not paid for by year end. Under accrual they are an expense and a liability (payables), even if no cash has moved.

manas.q: How are pending bills treated under accrual accounting?

children.note: Three examples using one made-up county, 'Mlima County', year ended 30 June 2025. Figures in KES millions.
Equitable share received 800. Rates billed 120, collected 90. Salaries paid 450. Supplies used 260, paid 180. Ambulance bought for 100 cash, life 5 years.
Receipts 800 + 90 = 890. Payments 450 + 180 + 100 = 730. Surplus of receipts over payments = 160.
Revenue 800 + 120 = 920. Expenses 450 + 260 + depreciation 20 (100 ÷ 5) = 730. Surplus = 190.
160 + 30 unpaid rates − 80 pending bills + 100 ambulance (an asset, not a cost) − 20 depreciation = 190.
Cash 160 + receivables 30 + ambulance 80 (100 − 20) = assets 270. Pending bills 80. Net assets 270 − 80 = 190 (starting from nil).
1 Mar 2025 a donor gives KES 50m to build a health centre; unspent money must be returned. By 30 June, KES 30m has been spent on the building.
Dr Bank 50m / Cr Grant liability (unmet conditions) 50m. No revenue yet because the county still owes the donor the work.
Dr Work in progress 30m / Cr Bank 30m. Then Dr Grant liability 30m / Cr Grant revenue 30m.
Revenue 30m in performance statement. Liability 20m still owed. Bank 50 − 30 = 20m. Checks: 50m in = 30m asset + 20m cash.
A grant with no conditions: Dr Bank 50m / Cr Grant revenue 50m at once.
Mlima's final budget (cash basis) vs actual, KES m. Variance = budget − actual for payments; actual − budget for receipts.
Equitable share: budget 800, actual 800, nil. Own-source revenue: budget 150, actual 90, 60 short. Total: 950 vs 890, 60 short.
Salaries 460 vs 450 (10 under). Goods and services 270 vs 180 (90 under). Development 220 vs 100 (120 under). Total 950 vs 730 (220 under).
Budget net 0, actual 160. Development absorption is only 100 ÷ 220 = 45%. The 90 'saving' on goods is false: 80 of bills are pending.

A cash surplus can hide large pending bills. Always check payables before praising a surplus.
A grant with conditions is a liability until the conditions are met. Only unconditional grants are revenue at once.
Under accrual, buying a road or vehicle creates an asset; only depreciation is the yearly expense.
IPSAS 47 replaced the older revenue standards (IPSAS 9 and 23). Older study packs and videos may still use the old ones.
A sub-county paid KES 40m to suppliers but received invoices for KES 55m. What is the expense under cash and accrual?
Cash basis: 40m. Accrual basis: 55m. The 15m difference is pending bills, shown as a liability.
A KES 20m conditional grant is received; 25% of the work is done by year end. Revenue and liability?
Revenue 20m × 25% = 5m. Liability 20m − 5m = 15m. Entries: Dr Bank 20 / Cr Liability 20; Dr Liability 5 / Cr Revenue 5.
A ward road cost KES 120m and lasts 20 years (straight line). Yearly depreciation and value after 2 years?
120 ÷ 20 = 6m a year. After 2 years: 120 − 12 = 108m carrying amount.
Development budget KES 300m; actual spent 210m. Absorption rate and variance?
210 ÷ 300 = 70%. Under-spend 90m, to be explained in the appropriation account.

PFM means all the steps for handling government money: planning the budget, collecting revenue, spending, keeping accounts, reporting and audit.

This topic builds on CA26 Public Finance and Taxation (how government raises money) and CA34S4 topic 1, Public sector accounting with IPSAS (how the books are kept).
Article 201 sets five guiding ideas for all public money. Every later rule in this topic grows out of them.

Public finance must be open and accountable with public participation; taxes shared fairly; revenue shared fairly between national and county levels and across generations; money used prudently; and finances managed and reported clearly.

manas.q: Name the main principles of public finance in Article 201.

children.note: Citizens must be able to see the budget and give their views before it is passed, for example at county budget hearings in each ward.

children.topic: Fair sharing of burdens and benefits
children.note: Taxes should fall fairly, and spending should reach all areas and groups, including people who will live in the future (do not leave them only debt).
Spend carefully, avoid waste, and get value from every shilling.
Governments must keep proper accounts and publish clear reports so Parliament, assemblies and the public can check them.
Government money is kept in official funds. Money can only come out of them under a law passed by the assembly and with the Controller of Budget's approval.
The main national account. All money raised by or for the national government goes in, unless a law sends it elsewhere.

manas.q: What is the Consolidated Fund?

children.note: Each county's main account, set up under the Constitution. County own revenue (e.g. market fees, parking) and the county's equitable share are paid into it.

manas.q: What is a County Revenue Fund?

children.note: Counties get a share of nationally raised revenue (equitable share) plus some conditional grants for set purposes. They also collect their own revenue.
Money leaves a fund only under an Appropriation Act (or similar law) and after the Controller of Budget approves the withdrawal.

children.topic: 4. The budget cycle and its dates
children.note: The budget is made and used in clear stages every year. The PFM Act fixes deadlines so everyone knows what comes next.
Planning → Budget Policy Statement → estimates → approval → Appropriation Act → spending (implementation) → accounting, audit and evaluation. Then the cycle starts again.

manas.q: List the stages of the budget process under PFM Act s.35.

links.title: PFM Act Cap 412A, s.35 (Kenya Law, consolidated 25 Sep 2026)

children.topic: Budget Review and Outlook Paper: 30 Sep
children.note: Treasury reviews last year's actual results and the economy, and sends the BROP to Cabinet by 30 September (s.26).

manas.q: What is the deadline for the Budget Review and Outlook Paper (BROP)?

links.title: PFM Act Cap 412A, s.26 (Kenya Law, consolidated 25 Sep 2026)

children.note: The BPS sets out the national priorities and spending ceilings for next year. It goes to Parliament by 15 February (s.25).

manas.q: By when must the Budget Policy Statement go to Parliament?

links.title: PFM Act Cap 412A, s.25 (Kenya Law, consolidated 25 Sep 2026)

children.note: The county's version of the BPS. It must fit the BPS and goes to the county assembly by 7 March (s.117).

manas.q: By when does the County Fiscal Strategy Paper go to the county assembly?

links.title: PFM Act Cap 412A, s.117 (Kenya Law, consolidated 25 Sep 2026)

children.note: The detailed estimates go to the National Assembly by 30 April (s.37). County estimates go to the county assembly by 30 April (s.129).

manas.q: By when must budget estimates be submitted?

links.title: PFM Act Cap 412A, s.37 and s.129 (Kenya Law, consolidated 25 Sep 2026)

children.note: The Appropriation Bill must be assented to by 30 June (s.39), and county appropriation laws passed by 30 June (s.131), so money is ready on 1 July.

manas.q: By when must the Appropriation Act be in place?

links.title: PFM Act Cap 412A, s.39 and s.131 (Kenya Law, consolidated 25 Sep 2026)

children.note: Any appropriation not spent by the end of the financial year lapses (s.45). It cannot be carried forward; it must be voted again next year.

manas.q: What happens to unspent appropriations at year end?

links.title: PFM Act Cap 412A, s.45 (Kenya Law, consolidated 25 Sep 2026)

children.note: The PFM Act sets limits so governments do not overspend, borrow for the wrong things, or let the wage bill eat the budget.

At least 30% of the budget to development over the medium term; wage bill capped at a share of revenue set by regulations; borrow only for development; keep debt sustainable; manage fiscal risks; keep tax rates predictable.

manas.q: State the national fiscal responsibility principles in PFM s.15.

links.title: PFM Act Cap 412A, s.15 (Kenya Law, consolidated 25 Sep 2026)

children.note: Recurrent spending must not be more than the county's total revenue; at least 30% to development over the medium term; wage bill capped by regulations.

manas.q: What are the county fiscal responsibility rules in PFM s.107?

links.title: PFM Act Cap 412A, s.107 (Kenya Law, consolidated 25 Sep 2026)

children.note: Development spending builds lasting assets (roads, clinics, water pipes). Recurrent spending keeps things running each year (salaries, fuel, rent, drugs).

manas.q: What is the difference between development and recurrent spending?

children.note: Development spending ÷ total budget × 100 should be at least 30%. The law says 'over the medium term', so look at the trend over a few years, not one year alone.
Short-term borrowing is only for cash-flow gaps, and the overdraft cannot exceed 5% of the most recent audited national revenue (s.15(3)).

links.title: PFM Act Cap 412A, s.15(3) (Kenya Law, consolidated 25 Sep 2026)

children.note: While money is being spent, several people and offices check that it is spent lawfully and well.

An independent office holder (one 8-year term). Approves each withdrawal from public funds only if it is lawful, and reports to each House of Parliament every four months on how the budget is being used.

manas.q: What are the two key roles of the Controller of Budget?

children.note: The senior officer of each entity (e.g. a Principal Secretary). Answers to the National Assembly for using resources lawfully, as authorised, and in an effective, efficient, economical and transparent way, and keeps proper records.

manas.q: What is an accounting officer accountable for under PFM s.68?

links.title: PFM Act Cap 412A, s.68 (Kenya Law, consolidated 25 Sep 2026)

children.note: Every national government entity must have internal audit. It checks controls, risk and governance from inside and reports to management and the audit committee.

manas.q: What does PFM s.73 require?

links.title: PFM Act Cap 412A, s.73 (Kenya Law, consolidated 25 Sep 2026)

children.note: If extra money is needed during the year, government can spend first, then must seek approval within two months of the first withdrawal. Total extra spending cannot exceed 10% of the amount Parliament appropriated for the year.

manas.q: State the two limits on supplementary spending under Article 223.

children.note: Bills for goods or services received but not paid by year end. They hurt suppliers and distort the budget, so they should be listed, verified and planned for in the next budget. Accrual accounts show them clearly.

manas.q: What are pending bills?

children.note: In outline: if a county seriously and persistently breaks financial rules, the national Treasury can stop transfers to it, following the Constitution and PFM Act steps, and Parliament must approve. The county gets a chance to answer first.

links.title: PFM Act Cap 412A, ss.95–97 (Kenya Law, consolidated 25 Sep 2026)

children.note: After the year ends, governments must report what they did with the money, and the Auditor-General checks it.

The accounting officer prepares annual statements (appropriation accounts with variance reasons, debt, assets and liabilities, policies, performance) and sends them to the Auditor-General within two months of year end (Act 27 of 2026; check the current rule, checked 11 Nov 2026).

manas.q: By when must an accounting officer submit annual financial statements to the Auditor-General?

links.title: PFM Act Cap 412A, s.81 as amended by Act No. 27 of 2026 (Kenya Law, consolidated 25 Sep 2026)

children.note: Copies also go to the Controller of Budget, National Treasury and Commission on Revenue Allocation, and the statements are published.

links.title: PFM Act Cap 412A, s.81 (Kenya Law, consolidated 25 Sep 2026)

children.note: Older textbooks say three months. Act No. 27 of 2026 changed it to two months. In exams, say which rule you use.
National Treasury prepares the consolidated annual statements for national government in the formats set by the Public Sector Accounting Standards Board.

links.title: PFM Act Cap 412A, s.80 (Kenya Law, consolidated 25 Sep 2026)

children.note: Independent (one 8-year term). Within six months after year end, audits and reports on national and county governments and other public bodies, saying whether public money was used lawfully and effectively.

manas.q: Within how long must the Auditor-General report after year end?

children.note: Parliament or the county assembly must debate and act on the audit report within three months of receiving it.

manas.q: How soon must Parliament debate the Auditor-General's report?

children.note: Borrow only for development, keep debt at a level Parliament approves as sustainable, and report debt in the annual statements. The Auditor-General also audits public debt.

links.title: PFM Act Cap 412A, s.15 (Kenya Law, consolidated 25 Sep 2026)

children.note: Modern budgeting asks not just 'how much did we spend?' but 'what did we achieve?'.
Money is grouped by programmes (e.g. 'maternal health') with targets and results, instead of only by items like salaries and fuel. It links spending to outcomes.

manas.q: What is programme-based budgeting?

children.note: Economy: buy inputs at the lowest fair cost. Efficiency: get the most output from the inputs. Effectiveness: achieve the intended result.

manas.q: What are the 3 Es of value for money?

children.note: Economy: buying gloves through a framework contract at a lower price. Efficiency: cost per patient seen falls. Effectiveness: fewer mothers die in childbirth.
Kenya moved from IPSAS cash basis to IPSAS accrual from 1 July 2024, so statements now show pending bills, debt, pensions and assets. This gives a truer picture for decisions.
Three short exercises with real-looking KES figures. Work them yourself first, then check the steps.
Kilima County (made up) has revenue of KES 10,000m and plans recurrent KES 7,400m and development KES 2,600m. Does it pass the s.107 tests?
Equitable share 8,000m + own-source revenue 1,200m + conditional grants 800m = KES 10,000m.
Recurrent = salaries 4,500m + operations 2,900m = KES 7,400m. 7,400m ≤ 10,000m, so this test passes.
Development 2,600m ÷ total budget 10,000m × 100 = 26%. That is below 30%, so the plan fails the development rule.
30% of 10,000m = 3,000m. Move 400m from operations to projects: recurrent 7,000m, development 3,000m (30%). Total still 10,000m.
Parliament appropriated KES 3,500bn for the year. A first supplementary already spent KES 200bn. Treasury now wants another KES 180bn.
10% × 3,500bn = KES 350bn of extra spending for the whole year.
200bn already + 180bn new = KES 380bn. 380bn > 350bn, so the new request breaks the cap by KES 30bn.
Treasury can add at most 350bn − 200bn = KES 150bn more, unless a law for special circumstances allows otherwise.
If the first extra withdrawal was on 15 January, approval must be sought by about 15 March (within two months).
Put the key dates in order for the year 1 July 2027 – 30 June 2028.
BROP to Cabinet by 30 Sep 2026 → BPS to Parliament by 15 Feb 2027 → County Fiscal Strategy Paper by 7 Mar 2027 → estimates by 30 Apr 2027 → Appropriation Act by 30 Jun 2027.
Spending starts 1 Jul 2027. The Controller of Budget approves withdrawals and reports every four months. Unspent money lapses on 30 Jun 2028.
Annual statements to the Auditor-General by 31 Aug 2028 (two months) → audit report by 31 Dec 2028 (six months) → Parliament debates within three months of receiving it.
Small slips in dates and limits cost easy marks. Watch these.

children.topic: Mixing up the BPS and BROP
children.note: BROP (30 Sep) looks back and to Cabinet; BPS (15 Feb) sets priorities and goes to Parliament.
Annual statements now go to the Auditor-General within two months (Act 27 of 2026). Check the current rule before your exam.
The 30% rule is about development spending as a share of the total budget, not of recurrent spending.
The 10% supplementary cap covers all extra spending in the year added together, not each request alone.
The Controller of Budget checks money before it goes out and during the year. The Auditor-General checks after the year ends.
Appropriations lapse at 30 June. Money must be voted again in the next budget.
Short exam-style questions. Answer first, then open the steps.

children.topic: Q1: County with recurrent above revenue
children.note: A county has revenue KES 6,000m, recurrent KES 6,300m, development KES 1,500m. Which s.107 rules fail?
Recurrent 6,300m > revenue 6,000m: fails. Total budget 7,800m; development 1,500 ÷ 7,800 = 19.2%: below 30%, fails. It must cut recurrent and find funds for projects.

children.topic: Q2: Explain the Controller of Budget
children.note: Explain two functions of the Controller of Budget under Article 228. (4 marks)
1) Approves withdrawals from public funds only when lawful. 2) Reports to each House of Parliament every four months on budget implementation. Add: independent, single 8-year term.

children.topic: Q3: Value for money at a hospital
children.note: A county hospital spent KES 6,000,000 on outpatient services and saw 12,000 patients. Find cost per patient and say which E it measures.
6,000,000 ÷ 12,000 = KES 500 per patient. This measures efficiency (output per input). Effectiveness would need outcomes, e.g. patients cured.
